name: Tinosorb M (bisoctrizole)
lead: Bisoctrizole, marketed by BASF as Tinosorb M (INCI name methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol), is an ultraviolet filter described as a hybrid: it is a benzotriazole organic molecule supplied as microfine particles in water-based dispersions, so it is said to act both by absorbing and by scattering UV light.[1] It is used in sunscreens for broad UVA and UVB coverage.

Published research on the ingredient includes contact-allergy case reports and series, photopatch-testing recommendations, ex vivo skin studies of an organo-mineral sunblock, and environmental monitoring. Several dermatology reports attribute allergic reactions to Tinosorb M to decyl glucoside, a surfactant in the commercial dispersion, rather than the filter itself.[2][3]
infobox: Permitted in cosmetic sunscreens, up to 10 percent[1]
Not in the OTC monograph per the cited source[1]

paras: A Grokipedia summary describes bisoctrizole as a bis-benzotriazole with a methylene bridge, a white powder insoluble in water, and used as microfine particles. The same source reports that it is permitted in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan and has not been cleared by the US FDA.[1] Because that source is AI-generated, these details are provisional.
A 2003 study evaluated an organo-mineral broad-spectrum sunblock on two ex vivo skin models, using markers of UVB damage (sunburn cells, p53) and UVA damage (vimentin) to assess photoprotection.[4]

A 2007 case report described allergic contact dermatitis from the filter.[5] Later reports concluded that decyl glucoside, an alkyl glucoside surfactant in the dispersion, was the cause in affected patients, and a 2013 report called Tinosorb M containing decyl glucoside a frequent cause of allergic contact dermatitis in the study population.[2][3] Reviews of alkyl glucosides describe cases of allergy from their presence in leave-on products including sunscreens.[6] A separate study concluded that true photoallergy to sunscreens is rare.[7]
A 2018 study measured organic UV stabilisers and filters in sediment of the North and Baltic Seas as part of a hazard assessment.[8]
Clinical evidence consists of dermatology case reports and series on contact allergy and a photopatch-testing consensus.[2][3][5][9] No trials testing Tinosorb M for appearance outcomes were found.

card.summary: A hybrid organic/particulate UV filter in European and Asian sunscreens; reported contact allergies have been traced to a surfactant in its dispersion.
card.note: Not in the US OTC monograph per the cited source.

quick.overview:
Tinosorb M is a broad-spectrum UV filter supplied as fine particles. It is described as working through both absorption and scattering, and it appears in sunscreens sold in the EU and other regions.

The published literature is mostly allergy reports and lab or ex vivo work. No trials were found testing it alone on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Its benzotriazole structure absorbs UV and dissipates the energy as heat; particles are also said to scatter some light.
quick.risks: Dermatology reports describe allergic contact dermatitis, attributed in several cases to decyl glucoside in the dispersion. A 2010 study found true photoallergy to sunscreens to be rare.
